proofs.proof_tex:
Fix an array in \(\mathcal T_K(r)\), and let \(P_\theta\) denote the observable law of \(\mathcal O_K\) induced by the uniform cell probabilities and the conditional Bernoulli probabilities \(p_{dj}\).  A compatible causal law is obtained by choosing, separately in every cell \(j\), a coupling \(\pi_j\) of \(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_{0j})\) and \(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_{1j})\).  Thus, for the causal mismatch parameter
\[
 \tau(\pi)=\frac1K\sum_{j=1}^K
 \Pr_{\pi_j}\{Y(1)\ne Y(0)\},
\]
the identified set is
\[
 \Theta_I(P_\theta)=
 \left\{
 \frac1K\sum_{j=1}^K t_j:
 |p_{1j}-p_{0j}|\le t_j\le
 \min\{p_{0j}+p_{1j},,2-p_{0j}-p_{1j}\}
 \right\}.
\]
Indeed, if \(Q_j=\Pr_{\pi_j}\{Y(0)=Y(1)=1\}\), then
\[
 \Pr_{\pi_j}\{Y(1)\ne Y(0)\}=p_{0j}+p_{1j}-2Q_j,
\]
and the elementary nonnegativity constraints on the four binary atoms give
\[
 \max\{0,p_{0j}+p_{1j}-1\}\le Q_j\le\min\{p_{0j},p_{1j}\}.
\]
Conversely, every \(Q_j\) in this interval defines four nonnegative atoms with the prescribed marginals.  Hence the displayed cellwise interval, and therefore the displayed identified set, is sharp.  This is the binary extremal-coupling technique; in particular its lower endpoint is the observed-law functional
\[
 L_K=\frac1K\sum_{j=1}^K|p_{1j}-p_{0j}|.
\]
By the amplitude ordering and the sign restriction,
\[
 |p_{1j}-p_{0j}|=|b\theta_{1j}-a\theta_{0j}|
 =\begin{cases}
 a-b,&\theta_{0j}\theta_{1j}=1,\\
 a+b,&\theta_{0j}\theta_{1j}=-1,
 \end{cases}
 =a-b\theta_{0j}\theta_{1j}.
\]
Averaging and using the definition of \(\rho_K\) yields \(L_K=a-b\rho_K\).  Thus the equality between the causal sharp endpoint and the observed-law functional has been proved from the coupling constraints rather than imposed as a definition.

Under \(\Gamma_{K,q}\), the products \(W_j=\theta_{0j}\theta_{1j}\) are independent, take values in \(\{-1,1\}\), and satisfy
\[
 \Pr(W_j=w)=\frac{1+qw}{2},\qquad \mathbb EW_j=q,qquad
 \rho_K=K^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^K W_j.
\]
The interval \([-r+2s_K,r-2s_K]\) has length \(2r-4s_K\ge3r/2\), because \(s_K\le r/8\).  Since the correlation lattice has spacing \(2/K\), that interval contains a lattice point once \(2/K<3r/2\).  Hence \(\mathcal R_K^\circ(r)\ne\varnothing\) for all sufficiently large \(K\).

For completeness, the required concentration bound follows by a direct exponential-moment argument.  If
\(\psi_q(t)=\log\mathbb E\exp\{t(W_j-q)\}\), then \(\psi_q(0)=\psi_q'(0)=0\), while \(\psi_q''(t)\) is the variance of a random variable supported on \([-1,1]\) under an exponential tilt and is therefore at most one.  Taylor's formula gives \(\psi_q(t)\le t^2/2\).  Independence, Markov's inequality, and minimization at \(t=s_K\) give
\[
 \Gamma_{K,q}(\rho_K-q>s_K)
 \le \inf_{t>0}\exp\{-Kt s_K+Kt^2/2\}
 =\exp(-Ks_K^2/2).
\]
Applying the same calculation to \(-W_j\) proves
\[
 \Gamma_{K,q}(A_{K,q}^{\mathrm c})
 \le2\exp(-Ks_K^2/2)=\eta_K,
\]
uniformly in \(q\).  The conditioning event has positive probability even when this numerical upper bound exceeds one: because \(q\) itself is a correlation-lattice point and \(|q|<1\), every sign-product configuration with empirical mean \(q\) has positive \(\Gamma_{K,q}\)-mass and belongs to \(A_{K,q}\).

If \(q\in\mathcal R_K^\circ(r)\) and \(A_{K,q}\) occurs, then
\[
 |\rho_K|\le |q|+s_K\le r-s_K<r.
\]
The sign restriction holds by construction, so the conditional law is supported on \(\mathcal T_K(r)\).  The already proved endpoint identity gives, pointwise on that support,
\[
 |L_K-(a-bq)|=b|\rho_K-q|\le bs_K.
\]

It remains to check the boundary-safe projection.  On the interior interval, a nearest point of a lattice of spacing \(2/K\) is at distance at most \(1/K\).  Outside that interval, the first or last admissible lattice point is less than \(2/K\) from the corresponding interval endpoint.  Consequently, for all \(\rho\in[-r,r]\),
\[
 |q_K(\rho)-\rho|\le2s_K+2/K.
\]
The smaller-point tie rule makes \(q_K\) a piecewise-constant Borel function on the finite Voronoi partition of \([-r,r]\), hence measurable.  These arguments use, respectively, lattice geometry, an exponential-moment concentration calculation, and support conditioning.

Because each arm size is a positive integer,
\[
 n_0n_1(n_0+n_1)\ge1\cdot1\cdot2=2.
\]
The definitions of \(\lambda_K\) and \(\varepsilon_K\) therefore give
\[
 \varepsilon_K=\frac{n_0n_1(n_0+n_1)}{K^2}\ge\frac2{K^2}.
\]
If \(K\) failed to diverge, an infinite subsequence would satisfy \(K\le K_\star\) for some finite \(K_\star\), and the last display would give \(\varepsilon_K\ge2/K_\star^2\) on that subsequence, contradicting the assumed convergence \(\varepsilon_K\to0\).  Hence \(K\to\infty\).

Write
\[
 I_{ik}=\mathbf 1\{Z_{0i}=Z_{1k}\},\qquad
 W=\sum_{i=1}^{n_0}\sum_{k=1}^{n_1}I_{ik}.
\]
For the dependency neighborhood consisting of pairs sharing \(i\) or \(k\), the uniform-cell and arm-independence assumptions give \(\mathbb EI_{ik}=K^{-1}\), and any two distinct indicators in one neighborhood have joint mean \(K^{-2}\).  Thus the quantities in the cited Chen--Stein dependency-neighborhood lemma are
\[
 b_1=\frac{n_0n_1(n_0+n_1-1)}{K^2},\qquad
 b_2=\frac{n_0n_1(n_0+n_1-2)}{K^2}.
\]
Consequently
\[
 d_{\mathrm{TV}}\{\mathcal L(W),\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_K)\}
 \le2(b_1+b_2)\le4\varepsilon_K. \tag{1}
\]

Let \(B\) be the event that some cell hit by both arms contains at least three observations in total.  A union bound over two observations from one arm and one from the other yields
\[
 \Pr(B)\le
 \frac{\binom{n_0}{2}n_1+n_0\binom{n_1}{2}}{K^2}
 =\frac{n_0n_1(n_0+n_1-2)}{2K^2}\le\frac{\varepsilon_K}{2}. \tag{2}
\]
On \(B^{\mathrm c}\), every cross-arm matching pair is an exactly-one-per-arm cell, so \(M_K=W\).  Equations (1)--(2) imply
\[
 d_{\mathrm{TV}}\{\mathcal L(M_K),\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_K)\}
 \le4\varepsilon_K+\Pr(B). \tag{3}
\]

We next establish the marked factorization, rather than assuming sufficiency.  Under the unconditioned product mixture \(\Gamma_{K,q}\), for an exactly-one-per-arm cell and \(x,y\in\{-1,1\}\), conditional Bernoulli sampling gives
\[
 \Pr_q(X_0=x,X_1=y)
 =\frac14\mathbb E_q[(1+2ax\theta_0)(1+2by\theta_1)]
 =\frac{1+cqxy}{4}. \tag{4}
\]
Therefore \(S=X_0X_1\) has \(\Pr_q(S=s)=(1+cqs)/2\), and, given \(S\), the orientation \(X_0\) is fair and independent of \(q\).  Different one-one cells have independent signs.  A block occupied by only one arm has a law independent of \(q\), even with repeated observations, because the corresponding marginal latent sign is fair.  The occupancy pattern is also parameter free.

Define \(\mathsf K_K^{\to}\) deterministically by retaining \(M_K\) and the positive- and negative-mark counts.  Before shell conditioning, (4) says its law is a count with the parameter-free law of \(M_K\), independently marked with parameter \(q\).  Independent marking is a Markov kernel and therefore contracts total variation.  Shell conditioning changes the latent law, and hence every data pushforward, by exactly at most \(\Gamma_{K,q}(A_{K,q}^{\mathrm c})\le\eta_K\).  From (3),
\[
 \sup_q d_{\mathrm{TV}}\!\left(
 P^{\mathrm{mix}}_{K,q}\mathsf K_K^{\to},P^{\mathcal E}_{\lambda_K,q}
 \right)
 \le4\varepsilon_K+\Pr(B)+\eta_K
 \le5\varepsilon_K+\eta_K. \tag{5}
\]

For the reverse direction, couple an input Poisson count to a variable with the known, parameter-free law of \(M_K\) by assigning common mass \(\min\{\Pr(M_K=m),\Pr(N=m)\}\) at every \(m\), and distribute the two residual masses arbitrarily.  The mismatch probability is their total-variation distance.  Conditional on equality, sample the occupancy configuration from its known law given \(M_K\); assign the input marks to the one-one cells in a uniformly randomized order; sample their fair orientations; and sample all one-arm blocks from their fair-sign mixture.  On \(B\), use any fixed distribution.  Every operation is a finite Markov kernel depending only on the displayed known constants.  By (4), on the event of equal counts and \(B^{\mathrm c}\) this is exactly the unconditioned mixed full-data law.  Hence (3), (2), and then shell conditioning give
\[
 \sup_q d_{\mathrm{TV}}\!\left(
 P^{\mathcal E}_{\lambda_K,q}\mathsf K_K^{\leftarrow},P^{\mathrm{mix}}_{K,q}
 \right)
 \le(4\varepsilon_K+\Pr(B))+\Pr(B)+\eta_K
 \le5\varepsilon_K+\eta_K. \tag{6}
\]
Taking the minimum of the right sides with one proves the two kernel claims.  The target attached to both indexed laws is, by construction, \(a-bq\); the random realized endpoint under the mixture is not being redefined.

Finally fix a deterministic legal array and write \(t_j=\theta_{0j}\theta_{1j}\).  Conditional on \(M_K=m\), a uniform random ordering of the one-one cell labels is sampling without replacement from \(\{1,\ldots,K\}\).  Given label \(j\), conditional outcome independence gives a mark of mean
\[
 \mathbb E(S\mid j)=(2a\theta_{0j})(2b\theta_{1j})=ct_j. \tag{7}
\]
Couple the ordered sample without replacement to \(m\) independent uniform labels.  They agree unless the latter labels repeat, an event of probability at most \(m(m-1)/(2K)\).  Under independent labels, (7) gives independent marks with mean \(cK^{-1}\sum_jt_j=c\rho_K\).  Distinct collision indicators \(I_{ik}\) are pairwise independent, including when they share one observation, and hence
\[
 \mathbb E[M_K(M_K-1)]\le\mathbb E[W(W-1)]
 =\frac{n_0n_1(n_0n_1-1)}{K^2}\le\lambda_K^2. \tag{8}
\]
Averaging the without-replacement coupling error and combining it with (3) gives
\[
 d_{\mathrm{TV}}\!\left(
 \mathcal L_\theta(M_K,S_1,\ldots,S_{M_K}),
 \mathcal E_{\lambda_K,\rho_K}
 \right)
 \le4\varepsilon_K+\Pr(B)+\frac{\lambda_K^2}{2K}
 \le5\varepsilon_K+\frac{\lambda_K^2}{2K}.
\]
This calculation is independent of the particular deterministic signs, proving uniformity.

Put
\[
 \delta_K=2s_K+2/K,
 \qquad
 \omega_K=\min\{1,\lambda_Kc\delta_K/2\},
 \qquad
 d_K=\min\{1,5\varepsilon_K+\lambda_K^2/(2K)\}.
\]
We may clip every endpoint estimator to \(\mathcal A\), because the target lies in \(\mathcal A\); this cannot increase absolute loss and makes the loss bounded by \(2br\).

For the upper comparison, apply a marked-Poisson rule within \(\zeta>0\) of its minimax infimum to the deterministic collision statistic.  The deterministic part of the collision-comparison theorem and total-variation contraction of bounded expectations, followed by \(\zeta\downarrow0\), give
\[
 R_K\le R(\lambda_K)+2br\,d_K. \tag{9}
\]
For the reverse comparison, apply a finite-array rule within \(\zeta>0\) of its minimax infimum after \(\mathsf K_K^{\leftarrow}\), and let \(\zeta\downarrow0\) after the bound.  Given \(\rho\in[-r,r]\), use only in the analysis the lattice point \(q=q_K(\rho)\).  The common-count, independent-mark coupling has mismatch probability at most
\[
 \lambda_K\left|\frac{1+c\rho}{2}-\frac{1+cq}{2}\right|
 \le\omega_K. \tag{10}
\]
Under \(\Pi_{K,q}^{\mathrm{shell}}\), the realized endpoint differs from \(a-bq\) by at most \(bs_K\), while \(|(a-bq)-(a-b\rho)|\le b\delta_K\).  The reverse comparison, (10), and the triangle inequality for absolute loss therefore imply
\[
 R(\lambda_K)\le R_K+b(s_K+\delta_K)+2br(e_K+\omega_K). \tag{11}
\]
These inequalities are obtained before taking the decision infima; randomization is preserved by composition of Markov kernels.

Suppose \(\lambda_K\to\lambda<\infty\).  The growing-cells lemma gives \(K\to\infty\), whence \(s_K\to0\), \(Ks_K^2\to\infty\), and \(\eta_K\to0\).  Thus \(e_K,d_K,\delta_K,\omega_K\to0\).  Finally, couple Poisson counts of intensities \(\lambda\) and \(\lambda'\) by adding an independent \(\operatorname{Poisson}(|\lambda-\lambda'|)\) count and mark the added points under the same \(\rho\).  Uniformly in \(\rho\), the resulting laws on the common count space differ with probability at most \(1-e^{-|\lambda-\lambda'|}\le|\lambda-\lambda'|\).  Applying the same rule on that common space at both intensities and using the \(2br\) loss bound proves continuity of \(R(\lambda)\).  Hence (9)--(11) imply \(R_K\to R(\lambda)\).  The lower comparison used only mixtures supported on legal deterministic arrays and explicitly paid for the random-to-fixed target discrepancy; the upper comparison used only the collision statistic and the realized \(L_K\).

We first prove the two-sided experiment transfer.  Let
\[
 \delta_K=2s_K+2/K,
 \quad
 u_K=e_K+\min\{1,\lambda_Kc\delta_K/2\},
 \quad
 d_K=\min\{1,5\varepsilon_K+\lambda_K^2/(2K)\}.
\]
Start with a finite-array interval rule having uniform coverage \(1-\alpha\) and worst expected length within an arbitrary \(\zeta>0\) of \(C_{K,\alpha}\), and apply it after the parameter-free reverse kernel.  For analysis at \(\rho\), put \(q=q_K(\rho)\).  Under the supported mixture, coverage of the random realized \(L_K\) is at least \(1-\alpha\), and \(|L_K-(a-bq)|\le bs_K\).  Expand both interval endpoints by \(b(s_K+\delta_K)\), clipped to \(\mathcal A\).  Common Poisson counts and common-uniform coupling of each pair of Bernoulli marks give
\[
 d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P_{\lambda_K,\rho},P_{\lambda_K,q})
 \le\min\{1,\lambda_Kc|\rho-q|/2\}
 \le\min\{1,\lambda_Kc\delta_K/2\}.
\]
Together with the reverse comparison, this shows, uniformly in \(\rho\), that the expanded interval covers \(a-b\rho\) with probability at least \(1-\alpha-u_K\), and its expected length is at most
\[
 C_{K,\alpha}+\zeta+2b(s_K+\delta_K)+2br\,u_K. \tag{12}
\]
If a rule has coverage \(1-\alpha-u\), mixing it with the full interval with probability
\(\gamma=u/(\alpha+u)\) gives coverage
\[
 \gamma+(1-\gamma)(1-\alpha-u)=1-\alpha. \tag{13}
\]
The extra expected length is at most \(2br\gamma\).  Letting \(\zeta\downarrow0\) in (12)--(13) proves
\[
 C_\alpha(\lambda_K)\le C_{K,\alpha}
 +2b(s_K+\delta_K)+2br\,u_K
 +\frac{2br\,u_K}{\alpha+u_K}. \tag{14}
\]

Conversely, apply a marked-Poisson honest rule to the deterministic collision statistic.  Total variation at most \(d_K\) reduces coverage by at most \(d_K\) and changes a \([0,2br]\)-valued expected length by at most \(2brd_K\).  The repair (13), now with \(u=d_K\), is a single randomization independent of the array.  Therefore
\[
 C_{K,\alpha}\le C_\alpha(\lambda_K)+2brd_K
 +\frac{2brd_K}{\alpha+d_K}. \tag{15}
\]
For two intensities, add an independent Poisson count of mean \(|\lambda-\lambda'|\) to the smaller count and mark the added points under the same \(\rho\).  The two laws on the common count space then disagree with probability at most \(1-e^{-|\lambda-\lambda'|}\).  Applying the same interval rule at both intensities and then using (13) proves continuity of \(C_\alpha(\lambda)\).  If \(\lambda_K\to\lambda<\infty\), then \(K\to\infty\), \(s_K\to0\), \(Ks_K^2\to\infty\), and hence \(\eta_K,\delta_K,u_K,d_K\to0\).  Equations (14)--(15) thus give \(C_{K,\alpha}\to C_\alpha(\lambda)\).  This proves honesty for the realized target before any limit is taken.

We next certify the finite programs.  For the lower bound, take an arbitrary continuum-honest interval rule.  On every retained state replace its interval by the convex hull of the grid targets it contains, or the null pattern if there is no such target.  Membership of each grid target is preserved and length cannot increase.  Deleting the overflow states removes at most \(\tau_m\) coverage.  Hence this rule is feasible for the exact lower relaxation with objective no larger than its continuum objective.  The outward directions in the corrected construction only enlarge that feasible set and decrease its recorded objective.  Exact rational weak duality consequently gives
\[
D_{m,h,s}^-\le C_\alpha(\lambda). \tag{16}
\]

The advertised tail certificate is also derived rather than inherited from the construction.  If \(\lambda=0\), then \(\tau_m(0)=0\).  If \(0<\lambda<m+1\), exponential Markov inequality gives, for \(t>0\),
\[
 \Pr(N\ge m+1)
 \le\exp\{\lambda(e^t-1)-t(m+1)\}.
\]
The minimizing positive value is \(t=\log((m+1)/\lambda)\), and substitution yields
\[
 \tau_m(\lambda)\le
 e^{-\lambda}\left(\frac{e\lambda}{m+1}\right)^{m+1}.
\]

For the upper bound, exact rational primal feasibility implies actual gridwise coverage because coverage probabilities were rounded downward and its right side upward; the expected-length coefficients were rounded upward.  Give the overflow state the action \(\mathcal A\).  If \(\rho_j\) is nearest to \(\rho\), then \(|\rho-\rho_j|\le h/2\).  Expansion by \(bh/2\) on each endpoint makes inclusion of \(a-b\rho_j\) imply inclusion of \(a-b\rho\).  The common-count mark coupling gives
\[
 d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P_{\lambda,\rho},P_{\lambda,\rho_j})
 \le\lambda c|\rho-\rho_j|/2\le\omega_h.
\]
Thus off-grid coverage is at least \(1-\alpha-\omega_h\); (13) with \(u=\omega_h\) repairs it.  Expansion adds at most \(bh\), changing the sampling parameter changes expected length by at most \(2br\omega_h\), and repair adds at most \(2br\gamma_h\).  Directed upper rounding proves
\[
 C_\alpha(\lambda)\le U_{m,h,s}^+. \tag{17}
\]

It remains to establish contraction rather than merely validity.  A continuum rule within \(\zeta\) of the infimum can be changed to report \(\mathcal A\) on the overflow state, at cost at most \(2br\tau_m\).  Rounding its two endpoints outward to adjacent action-grid endpoints adds at most \(2bh\) and preserves coverage.  This produces feasible exact upper actions whose value tends to \(C_\alpha(\lambda)\).  In the other direction, an exact lower-LP rule can report \(\mathcal A\) on overflow, expand by one mesh, and use (13); its resulting excess length is bounded by a constant multiple of
\[
 \tau_m+bh+\omega_h.
\]
The aggregate rounding condition (A) changes coverage and expected length by at most a constant multiple of \(2^{-s}\); one more use of (13) repairs the coverage part.  Since the Poisson tail tends to zero as \(m\to\infty\), all these errors, and then \(\zeta\), vanish along every declared refinement.  Combining this fact with (16)--(17) yields
\[
 U_{m,h,s}^+-D_{m,h,s}^-\longrightarrow0,
 \qquad
 D_{m,h,s}^-,U_{m,h,s}^+\longrightarrow C_\alpha(\lambda).
\]
All optimization variables, row-sum constraints, coverage constraints, length constraints, overflow action, and off-grid repairs are therefore explicit and finitely checkable.

First note consequences of the sparse assumptions that will be used in divisions and limits.  Since the arm sizes are positive integers,
\[
 \varepsilon_K=\frac{n_0n_1(n_0+n_1)}{K^2}
 \ge\frac{n_d^2}{K^2}\quad(d=0,1).
\]
Thus \(n_d/K\to0\).  Moreover
\[
 \frac{\lambda_K^2/K}{\varepsilon_K}
 =\frac{n_0n_1}{K(n_0+n_1)}
 \le\frac{\min(n_0,n_1)}K\longrightarrow0,
\]
so \(\lambda_K^2/K\to0\).  The deterministic comparison error \(d_K\) therefore tends to zero.

In \(\mathcal E_{\lambda_K,\rho}\), conditional on \(N=m\), the marks are independent with
\[
 \mu_\rho=\mathbb ES_\ell=c\rho,qquad
 \sigma_\rho^2=1-c^2\rho^2\ge1-c^2r^2>0. \tag{18}
\]
The strict lower bound follows from \(a,b<1/2\), hence \(c<1\), and \(r<1\).  The elementary characteristic-function expansion for bounded centered marks is uniform for \(\rho\in[-r,r]\): for fixed \(t\),
\[
 \mathbb E_\rho\exp\left\{
 it\frac{S-\mu_\rho}{\sigma_\rho\sqrt m}
 \right\}
 =1-\frac{t^2}{2m}+O(m^{-3/2}),
\]
where the remainder is uniform by (18).  Raising to the \(m\)-th power proves the uniform conditional central limit theorem.  Also \(N/\lambda_K\to1\) in probability because
\[
 \Pr\{|N/\lambda_K-1|>\epsilon\}
 \le\frac1{\epsilon^2\lambda_K},
\]
uniformly because the count law is parameter free, and \(\Pr(N=0)=e^{-\lambda_K}\to0\).  On \(N>0\), factor the studentized quantity as
\[
 \frac{\sqrt N(\overline S-c\rho)}{\sigma_\rho}\,
 \sqrt{\frac{\lambda_K}{N}}\,
 \frac{\sigma_\rho}{\sqrt{1-\overline S^2+N^{-1}}}.
\]
The first factor has the uniform conditional Gaussian limit, and the last two converge uniformly in probability to one.  Therefore
\[
 \frac{\sqrt{\lambda_K}(\overline S-c\rho)}
 {\sqrt{1-\overline S^2+N^{-1}}}
 \rightsquigarrow\mathcal N(0,1),
 \qquad
 \overline S-c\rho\to0
\]
uniformly in \(\rho\in[-r,r]\).  Since \(c=4ab\),
\[
 \widehat L_K-(a-b\rho)
 =-\frac{\overline S-c\rho}{4a},
 \qquad
 \widehat V_K- V(\rho)
 =\frac{-\overline S^2+c^2\rho^2+N^{-1}}{16a^2}. \tag{19}
\]
Equations (18)--(19) prove the asserted studentized limit and variance consistency in the marked experiment.  On \(N=0\), the declared fixed positive default makes the quotient well defined, and this event is harmless because its probability is \(e^{-\lambda_K}\to0\).

For every deterministic array, the collision statistic has total-variation distance at most \(d_K\to0\) from this marked experiment at \(\rho=\rho_K\).  Total variation controls every event, so the convergence in (19), its uniformity, and variance consistency transfer without any moment argument.  Substituting the standard-normal quantile in the transferred studentized convergence yields
\[
 \inf_{\theta\in\mathcal T_K(r)}
 \Pr_\theta\left\{
 L_K\in\left[\widehat L_K\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}
 \sqrt{\widehat V_K/\lambda_K}\right]
 \right\}=1-\alpha+o(1).
\]
No projection is used, so there is no boundary atom.  This is a random-count characteristic-function argument followed by a uniform total-variation transfer.

Let \(g^{\mathrm{step}}_{d,K,\theta}(u)=p_{d,\kappa_K(u)}\).  The union of the \(K-1\) interpolation strips has Lebesgue measure at most \(2(K-1)K^{-3}\le2K^{-2}\).  On a strip of half-width \(w=K^{-3}\), the integral of the absolute difference between the affine connector and the step function is one half of \(w|p_{d,j+1}-p_{dj}|\), and hence is at most \(a_dK^{-3}\), where \(a_0=a\) and \(a_1=b\).  Summing the strips gives
\[
 \int_0^1|g_{d,K,\theta}(u)-g^{\mathrm{step}}_{d,K,\theta}(u)|\,du
 \le\frac{a_d}{K^2}. \tag{28}
\]

Couple a continuous observation and its step version by using the same uniform \(U_{di}\), the same label \(\kappa_K(U_{di})\), and a common uniform random variable to generate the two Bernoulli outcomes.  The mismatch probability for one observation is the integral in (28).  A union bound over observations and then data processing by \(\mathsf Q_K\) yield the stronger estimate
\[
 \sup_\theta
 \lVert P^{\mathrm c}_{K,\theta}\mathsf Q_K-P^{\mathcal F}_{K,\theta}\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}
 \le\frac{n_0a+n_1b}{K^2}
 \le\frac{2(n_0+n_1)}{K^2}. \tag{29}
\]
In the opposite direction, a parameter-free kernel that adds an independent uniform position within each observed cell turns the discrete experiment into the step experiment; the same coupling proves the corresponding deficiency bound in (29).  This is a comparison through kernels, not a claim that probability measures on the raw, different sample spaces have a direct total-variation distance.

The binary extremal-coupling calculation from the endpoint proposition applies pointwise in \(u\), so
\[
 L_K^{\mathrm c}=\int_0^1|g_{1,K,\theta}(u)-g_{0,K,\theta}(u)|\,du.
\]
The reverse triangle inequality and (28) give
\[
 |L_K^{\mathrm c}-L_K|
 \le\sum_{d=0}^1\int_0^1
 |g_{d,K,\theta}-g^{\mathrm{step}}_{d,K,\theta}|\,du
 \le\frac{a+b}{K^2}
 \le\frac{2(a+b)}{K^2}. \tag{30}
\]
Both bounds are uniform in the signs.

Composing any discrete rule with \(\mathsf Q_K\), or any continuous rule with the uniform-within-cell reverse kernel, changes a bounded risk or a coverage probability by at most the error in (29); expanding an interval by the target error in (30) and using the full-interval repair preserves honesty.  Under finite collision intensity these errors vanish because \(n_0+n_1\le K^2\varepsilon_K/(n_0n_1)\le K^2\varepsilon_K\).  In the sparse Gaussian regime, (30) is negligible after multiplication by \(\sqrt{\lambda_K}\), since \(\lambda_K/K\to0\), while (29) still tends to zero because \((n_0+n_1)/K^2\le\varepsilon_K\).  Thus the finite-collision decision conclusions and the sparse Gaussian conclusion transfer at the actual \(L_K^{\mathrm c}\) under their stated error conditions.  The construction and both kernels are defined only on \(\mathcal I_K(r)\), so no extension to a larger smoothness class is asserted.

theorem.proof_tex:
We give the local lower and upper arguments separately and keep the order of limits explicit.

First derive the local limit experiment.  Put \(u_+=1+c\rho_0\), \(u_-=1-c\rho_0\), both strictly positive, and
\[
 I_0=\frac{c^2}{1-c^2\rho_0^2}.
\]
Under \(\mathcal E_{\lambda_K,\rho_0}\), the two mark counts are independent Poisson variables with means \(\lambda_Ku_+/2\) and \(\lambda_Ku_-/2\).  For \(\rho=\rho_0+h/\sqrt{\lambda_K}\), Taylor expansion of the exact likelihood gives, uniformly for \(h\) in a fixed compact set,
\[
 \log\frac{f_{\lambda_K,\rho}}{f_{\lambda_K,\rho_0}}
 =h\Delta_K-\frac12h^2I_0+o_{P_{\rho_0}}(1), \tag{20}
\]
where
\[
 \Delta_K=\frac c{\sqrt{\lambda_K}}
 \left(\frac{N_+}{u_+}-\frac{N_-}{u_-}\right),
 \qquad
 \mathbb E_{\rho_0}\Delta_K=0,qquad
 \operatorname{Var}_{\rho_0}(\Delta_K)=I_0.
\]
The centered Poisson characteristic functions show \(\Delta_K\rightsquigarrow\mathcal N(0,I_0)\).  The third-order Taylor remainder in (20) is \(O_{P}(\lambda_K^{-1/2})\) on compact \(h\)-sets because \(u_\pm>0\).  If \(\Lambda_{K,h}\) is the likelihood ratio in (20), direct evaluation of the two Poisson exponential moments gives
\[
 \mathbb E_{\rho_0}\Lambda_{K,h}^2
 =\exp\left\{\frac{c^2h^2}{2}
 \left(\frac1{u_+}+\frac1{u_-}\right)\right\}
 =e^{h^2I_0}.
\]
Thus the likelihood ratios are uniformly integrable on every compact \(h\)-set.  Hence, for every finite collection of local \(h\)'s, the likelihood-ratio vector converges in \(L^1\) to that of the Gaussian shift experiment
\[
 X=-bh+\sqrt{V(\rho_0)}Z,\qquad Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1), \tag{21}
\]
for estimating the local target \(-bh\), because
\[
 \frac{b^2}{I_0}=\frac{1-c^2\rho_0^2}{16a^2}=V(\rho_0). \tag{22}
\]
For clarity, finite-prior risk convergence used below follows directly from this \(L^1\) statement.  Dominating all laws by the central law, the Bayes risk under a finite prior is the expectation of the pointwise infimum, over the action, of a finite weighted sum of bounded losses times likelihood ratios.  This infimum is Lipschitz in the likelihood-ratio vector with constant at most \(T\).  Thus its expectations converge by \(L^1\), with no appeal to unbounded-loss convergence.  The scaled image \(\sqrt{\lambda_K}(\mathcal D-(a-b\rho_0))\) exhausts \(\mathbb R\), because \(\rho_0\in(-r,r)\) and \(\mathcal A\subset\mathcal D\); restricting finite-sample actions to this image can only increase the lower Bayes bound and does not alter the limit.

We next compute the minimax value of (21) for \(\ell_T\).  Let \(Z_V\sim\mathcal N(0,V(\rho_0))\), and denote its density by \(\varphi_V\).  Put
\[
 m_T=\mathbb E\min\{Z_V^2,T\}.
\]
The translation-equivariant estimator \(X\) has constant risk \(m_T\).  Conversely, average the risk of any estimator against a uniform prior for the location on \([-A,A]\).  For \(|x|\le A-B\), the inner convolution contains all errors in \([-B,B]\); hence the average risk is at least
\[
 \left(1-\frac BA\right)
 \inf_v\int_{-B}^{B}\ell_T(v+z)\varphi_V(z)\,dz. \tag{23}
\]
Let first \(A\to\infty\), then \(B\to\infty\).  The layer-cake identity
\[
 \ell_T(x)=\int_0^T\mathbf 1\{|x|>\sqrt t\}\,dt
\]
and symmetry and unimodality of the Gaussian density show that every centered interval has maximal Gaussian probability; therefore the last infimum tends to its value at \(v=0\), namely \(m_T\).  Continuous uniform priors in (23) can be approximated by finite grids because Gaussian shift laws are continuous in total variation and the bounded loss is continuous.  Consequently, for every \(\epsilon>0\), there is a finite prior supported in some \([-G,G]\) whose Gaussian Bayes risk is at least \(m_T-\epsilon\).

We now transfer this finite prior to legal deterministic arrays.  Positivity of both arm sizes gives
\[
 \varepsilon_K\ge (n_d/K)^2\quad(d=0,1),
 \qquad
 \lambda_K/K=(n_0/K)(n_1/K)\to0.
\]
Eventually
\[
 s_K=(K\lambda_K)^{-1/4},\qquad
 \sqrt{\lambda_K}s_K=(\lambda_K/K)^{1/4}\to0,qquad
 Ks_K^2=\sqrt{K/\lambda_K}\to\infty. \tag{24}
\]
Thus \(\eta_K\to0\), and also
\[
 \sqrt{\lambda_K}\sup_{|h|\le G}
 \left|q_K(\rho_0+h/\sqrt{\lambda_K})-\rho_0-h/\sqrt{\lambda_K}\right|\to0. \tag{25}
\]
For each support point \(h\) of the finite prior, use
\(\Pi_{K,q_K(\rho_0+h/\sqrt{\lambda_K})}^{\mathrm{shell}}\).  By (24)--(25), for every fixed \(H>G+1\), all arrays in these mixture supports belong to \(\mathcal H_K(\rho_0,H)\) for all sufficiently large \(K\).  Their scaled realized-target discrepancy satisfies
\[
 \sup\sqrt{\lambda_K}|L_K-(a-bq_K)|
 \le b\sqrt{\lambda_K}s_K\to0. \tag{26}
\]
Because \(\ell_T\) is \(2\sqrt T\)-Lipschitz, (26) changes risk by \(o(1)\) at fixed \(T\).  The reverse kernel is common to all \(q\)'s, and its total-variation error is \(e_K\to0\) by (24).  Hence every full-data rule induces one marked-Poisson rule whose finite-prior Bayes risk is no larger than the full-data mixture risk plus \(Te_K+o(1)\).  The mixture risk is bounded above by the supremum over the deterministic shell.  Equations (20)--(26) and finite-prior convergence therefore give
\[
 \liminf_{K\to\infty}\inf_{D_K}
 \sup_{\mathcal H_K(\rho_0,H)}
 \mathbb E\ell_T(\sqrt{\lambda_K}(D_K-L_K))
 \ge m_T-\epsilon
\]
for every fixed \(T\) and all sufficiently large fixed \(H>G+1\).  Letting \(H\to\infty\) and then \(\epsilon\downarrow0\) proves the lower bound \(m_T\).

For the upper bound, the uniform sparse Gaussian theorem and bounded continuity of \(\ell_T\) imply, for every fixed \(H,T\),
\[
 \limsup_{K\to\infty}\sup_{\mathcal H_K(\rho_0,H)}
 \mathbb E\ell_T\!\left(
 \sqrt{\lambda_K}(\widehat L_K-L_K)
 \right)\le m_T. \tag{27}
\]
The distance from \(a-b\rho_0\) to the boundary of \(\mathcal D=[a-b,a+b]\) is positive.  On a fixed shell, consistency makes clipping asymptotically inactive, so (27) also holds for \(\operatorname{clip}_{\mathcal D}(\widehat L_K)\).  Combining the lower and upper bounds, then taking \(H\to\infty\), and only afterward using monotone convergence as \(T\to\infty\), gives
\[
 \lim_{T\to\infty}m_T=\mathbb EZ_V^2=V(\rho_0),
\]
which is the asserted ordered identity.  At no stage was an unbounded scaled loss transferred in total variation.

added_lemmas.statement:
Let \(\{I_\gamma:\gamma\in\mathcal G\}\) be a finite family of Bernoulli random variables, let \(B_\gamma\subseteq\mathcal G\) be dependency neighborhoods such that \(I_\gamma\) is independent of \(\{I_\zeta:\zeta\notin B_\gamma\}\), and put
\[
 W=\sum_{\gamma\in\mathcal G}I_\gamma,\qquad
 \mu=\mathbb EW,qquad
 b_1=\sum_{\gamma\in\mathcal G}\sum_{\zeta\in B_\gamma}
       \mathbb EI_\gamma\,\mathbb EI_\zeta,qquad
 b_2=\sum_{\gamma\in\mathcal G}\sum_{\substack{\zeta\in B_\gamma\\\zeta\ne\gamma}}
       \mathbb E(I_\gamma I_\zeta).
\]
Then, for total variation defined as the supremum over measurable events,
\[
 d_{\mathrm{TV}}\!\left(\mathcal L(W),\operatorname{Poisson}(\mu)\right)
 \le 2(b_1+b_2).
\]

source.locator: Theorem 1, first total-variation bound, specialized to dependency neighborhoods with the supremum-over-events convention

attestation.note: The frozen bibliography supplies the publication and theorem locator; this node records only the weaker dependency-neighborhood consequence used in the collision proof.

proposed_definition_changes.proposed:
Fix integers \(m,s\ge1\) and a grid \(G_h=\{-r=\rho_0<\cdots<\rho_J=r\}\) of rational or computable-real nodes with maximum adjacent gap at most \(h\).  Let \(\mathsf X_m=\{(k,l)\in\mathbb N_0^2:k+l\le m\}\), append an overflow state \(\star\), and put \(\tau_m(\lambda)=\Pr\{\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda)>m\}\).  If \(m+1>\lambda\), then the Chernoff calculation
\[
 \tau_m(\lambda)\le\overline\tau_m(\lambda):=
 e^{-\lambda}\left(\frac{e\lambda}{m+1}\right)^{m+1}
\]
certifies the discarded mass.  Its worst effects are at most \(\overline\tau_m\) on coverage and \(2br\overline\tau_m\) on expected length.

The finite action grid is
\[
 \mathsf A_h=\{[a-b\rho_v,a-b\rho_u]:0\le u\le v\le J\}.
\]
The lower relaxation additionally admits a null grid-coverage pattern of length zero.  For any \(\rho,\rho'\in[-r,r]\), common Poisson counts and common-uniform-coupled Bernoulli marks give
\[
 \lVert f_{\lambda,\rho}-f_{\lambda,\rho'}\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}
 \le\omega_\lambda(|\rho-\rho'|):=min\{1,\lambda c|\rho-\rho'|/2\}.
\]
Thus a fixed event has this probability modulus and a \([0,2br]\)-valued length has expectation modulus \(2br\omega_\lambda\).

For the lower program let \(\mathsf A_h^-=\mathsf A_h\cup\{\varnothing_G\}\), where \(\varnothing_G\) has zero length and covers no grid target.  With \(t_j=a-b\rho_j\), its exact-coefficient form is
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \operatorname*{minimize}_{t,(w_{x,A})}\quad &t,\\
 \text{subject to}\quad&
 w_{x,A}\ge0,\qquad \sum_{A\in\mathsf A_h^-}w_{x,A}=1
 &&(x\in\mathsf X_m),\\
 &\sum_{x\in\mathsf X_m} f_{\lambda,\rho_j}(x)
   \sum_{\substack{A\in\mathsf A_h^-\\t_j\in A}}w_{x,A}
   \ge1-\alpha-\tau_m
 &&(0\le j\le J),\\
 &\sum_{x\in\mathsf X_m} f_{\lambda,\rho_j}(x)
   \sum_{A\in\mathsf A_h^-}\operatorname{len}(A)w_{x,A}
   \le t
 &&(0\le j\le J),\\
 &t\ge0.
 \end{aligned} \tag{L}
\]
It is a relaxation: an arbitrary interval is replaced by the shortest action spanning exactly the grid targets it contains, or by the null pattern if it contains none.  For the upper program set \(f_{\lambda,\rho_j}(\star)=\tau_m\), fix \(A_\star=\mathcal A\), and solve
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \operatorname*{minimize}_{t,(w_{x,A})}\quad &t,\\
 \text{subject to}\quad&
 w_{x,A}\ge0,\qquad \sum_{A\in\mathsf A_h}w_{x,A}=1
 &&(x\in\mathsf X_m),\\
 &\tau_m+\sum_{x\in\mathsf X_m} f_{\lambda,\rho_j}(x)
   \sum_{\substack{A\in\mathsf A_h\\t_j\in A}}w_{x,A}
   \ge1-\alpha
 &&(0\le j\le J),\\
 &2br\,\tau_m+\sum_{x\in\mathsf X_m} f_{\lambda,\rho_j}(x)
   \sum_{A\in\mathsf A_h}\operatorname{len}(A)w_{x,A}
   \le t
 &&(0\le j\le J),\\
 &t\ge0.
 \end{aligned} \tag{U}
\]

For computable inputs, the certification index \(s\) specifies an aggregate outward-rounding budget rather than merely a pointwise precision.  The procedure requests successively finer rational oracle brackets \(\lambda_s^-\le\lambda\le\lambda_s^+\), with \(\lambda_s^+-\lambda_s^-\le2^{-s}\), and corresponding brackets for every nonrational grid node and every other fixed real input, until directed interval evaluation returns rational bounds
\[
 f_{s,j,x}^-\le f_{\lambda,\rho_j}(x)\le f_{s,j,x}^+,
 \qquad
 \tau_{m,s}^-\le\tau_m(\lambda)\le\tau_{m,s}^+
 \le\overline\tau_m(\lambda_s^+),
\]
with
\[
 \max_j\left\{
 \sum_{x\in\mathsf X_m}(f_{s,j,x}^+-f_{s,j,x}^-)
 +(\tau_{m,s}^+-\tau_{m,s}^-)
 \right\}\le2^{-s}. \tag{A}
\]
The same aggregate budget is imposed on directed enclosures of the finitely many action lengths and correction terms.  Termination follows from computability and finiteness of each LP.  All right sides involving \(\alpha\) are rounded outward as well: the lower program uses the smaller right side and the upper program the larger right side.

In the rational lower relaxation, replace each coverage coefficient by \(f^+\), replace \(1-\alpha-\tau_m\) by a rational lower enclosure, and replace each length coefficient by a rational lower enclosure formed from \(f^-\) and a downward-rounded action length.  These directions enlarge the feasible set and decrease its recorded objective.  Let \(D_{m,h,s}^-\) be its exact rational optimum, certified by an exact rational dual optimum.  In the rational upper restriction, replace retained coverage coefficients by \(f^-\), the overflow coverage by \(\tau^-\), and \(1-\alpha\) by a rational upper enclosure; replace all retained and overflow length contributions by rational upper enclosures formed from \(f^+\), \(\tau^+\), and upward-rounded lengths.  For all sufficiently large \(s\) it is feasible; let \(P_{m,h,s}^+\) be its exact rational optimum, certified by an exact rational primal optimum.  Exact rational LP algorithms exist by finite pivoting or finite basis enumeration, so floating-point output is used only to propose a basis and never as a certificate.

Expand each retained upper action \(A=[L,U]\) to
\[
 E_h(A)=[\max\{a-br,L-bh/2\},\min\{a+br,U+bh/2\}].
\]
Put \(\omega_h=\min\{1,\lambda ch/4\}\) and \(\gamma_h=\omega_h/(\alpha+\omega_h)\).  Nearest-grid coverage implies coverage after expansion, up to an off-grid deficit \(\omega_h\); mixing with \(\mathcal A\) with probability \(\gamma_h\) repairs this deficit.  With every term replaced by its directed rational upper enclosure, report
\[
 U_{m,h,s}^+=P_{m,h,s}^++bh+2br\omega_h+2br\gamma_h,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{LP}_{m,h,s}^{\mathrm{int}}(\lambda)
 =[D_{m,h,s}^-,U_{m,h,s}^+].
\]
Then \(D_{m,h,s}^-\le C_\alpha(\lambda)\le U_{m,h,s}^+\).  Along every refinement with \(m\to\infty\), \(h\downarrow0\), \(s\to\infty\), and \(m+1>\lambda_s^+\), the tail, mesh, coverage-repair, and aggregate enclosure errors vanish.
proposed_definition_changes.reason: Pointwise coefficient enclosures and arbitrary feasible witnesses do not by themselves imply a shrinking bracket when the LP dimension grows. The corrected construction makes the reported endpoints exact rational optima and enforces an aggregate outward-rounding budget, which is the missing premise for refinement-uniform contraction.

proposed_definition_changes.proposed:
For \(M_K>0\), set
\[
 \overline S_K=M_K^{-1}\sum_{\ell=1}^{M_K}S_\ell,\qquad
 \widehat L_K=a-\frac{\overline S_K}{4a},\qquad
 \widehat V_K=\frac{1-\overline S_K^2+M_K^{-1}}{16a^2}.
\]
Use a fixed bounded default for \(\widehat L_K\) and a fixed positive default for \(\widehat V_K\) when \(M_K=0\).  Do not project \(\widehat L_K\) onto \(\mathcal A\).  The \(M_K^{-1}\) ridge makes \(\widehat V_K>0\) whenever \(M_K>0\) and vanishes in every regime in which \(M_K\to\infty\).
proposed_definition_changes.reason: The unregularized empirical mark variance can equal zero when all observed marks agree, leaving the displayed studentized statistic undefined. Adding a vanishing inverse-count ridge makes the divisor strictly positive and preserves the asserted variance limit.

proposed.statement:
There exist Markov kernels \(\mathsf K_K^{\to}:\mathcal O_K\rightsquigarrow\mathbb N_0^2\) and \(\mathsf K_K^{\leftarrow}:\mathbb N_0^2\rightsquigarrow\mathcal O_K\), depending only on \(K,n_0,n_1,a,b,r\) and not on \(q\), such that, with the same parameter \(q\in\mathcal R_K^{\circ}(r)\) indexing both experiments,
\[
\sup_q\lVert P^{\mathrm{mix}}_{K,q}\mathsf K_K^{\to}-P^{\mathcal E}_{\lambda_K,q}\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}\le e_K,\qquad \sup_q\lVert P^{\mathcal E}_{\lambda_K,q}\mathsf K_K^{\leftarrow}-P^{\mathrm{mix}}_{K,q}\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}\le e_K,
\]
where \(e_K=\min\{1,5\varepsilon_K+\eta_K\}\). Both sides attach the decision target \(a-bq\) to the index \(q\). Moreover, for every deterministic array in \(\mathcal T_K(r)\), the law of \((M_K,S_1,\ldots,S_{M_K})\) is within \(e_K^{\mathrm{det}}=\min\{1,5\varepsilon_K+\lambda_K^2/(2K)\}\) in total variation of \(\mathcal E_{\lambda_K,\rho_K}\), uniformly over arrays.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The proof invokes the published Chen--Stein dependency-neighborhood theorem, so the cited leaf must be a declared direct dependency.

proposed.statement: If \(\lambda_K\to\lambda\in[0,\infty)\), then \(R_K\to R(\lambda)\). The lower bound ranges over supported mixtures on legal deterministic arrays, and the upper bound uses only the deterministic collision statistic; both sides target the realized \(L_K\).

proposed_core_edits.reason: The reverse-risk proof directly uses the supported-mixture target-radius and legal-support conclusions, so that proposition is added as a direct dependency.

proposed.statement:
If \(\lambda_K\to\lambda\in[0,\infty)\), then \(C_{K,\alpha}\to C_\alpha(\lambda)\). For every computable \(\lambda\), every \(m,h\), and all sufficiently large certification precisions \(s\), the procedure \(\operatorname{LP}_{m,h,s}^{\mathrm{int}}(\lambda)\) returns exactly verified rational values satisfying
\[
D_{m,h,s}^-\le C_\alpha(\lambda)\le U_{m,h,s}^+.
\]
The upper rule uses the overflow action \(\mathcal A\), endpoint expansion \(E_h\), and full-interval repair probability \(\gamma_h\), and therefore has coverage at least \(1-\alpha\) for every \(\rho\in[-r,r]\), not only at grid points. Along any refinement with \(m\to\infty\), \(h\downarrow0\), \(s\to\infty\), and \(m+1>\lambda_s^+\), \(U_{m,h,s}^+-D_{m,h,s}^-\to0\) and both endpoints converge to \(C_\alpha(\lambda)\). Write \(d_K=\min\{1,5\varepsilon_K+\lambda_K^2/(2K)\}\). Applying the corrected upper rule through the deterministic collision statistic loses at most \(d_K\) in coverage; mixing once more with \(\mathcal A\) with probability \(d_K/(\alpha+d_K)\) restores coverage at least \(1-\alpha\) uniformly over \(\mathcal T_K(r)\) and adds at most \(2br\,d_K/(\alpha+d_K)\) in expected length. The matching lower certificate transfers through the supported-mixture reverse kernel, so the finite-array worst-case expected length converges to \(C_\alpha(\lambda)\).

proposed_core_edits.reason: The lower confidence transfer directly uses legal mixture support and the uniform realized-target radius, so that proposition is added as a direct dependency.

proposed.name: \widehat V_K
proposed.def: For \(M_K>0\), \(\widehat V_K=(1-\overline S_K^2+M_K^{-1})/(16a^2)\), where \(\overline S_K=M_K^{-1}\sum_{\ell=1}^{M_K}S_\ell\); use a fixed positive default when \(M_K=0\).

proposed_core_edits.reason: The symbol definition must match the corrected strictly positive collision studentizer.

proofs.proof_tex:
Write \(h(\rho)=a-b\rho\).  This is the target in the marked-Poisson experiment, whereas \(R(\lambda)\) and \(C_\alpha(\lambda)\) are the decision functionals of the observable law defined in \(\mathrm{def{:}poisson\mbox{-}decision\mbox{-}frontiers}\).  The declared ranges give \(b>0\), \(c>0\), \(0<r<1\), and \(cr<1\).  Consequently all mark probabilities are strictly positive, and every division below by \(b\), \(c\), or \(1-cx\), \(0\leq x\leq r\), is valid.

First take \(\lambda=0\).  By \(\mathrm{def{:}marked\mbox{-}poisson\mbox{-}experiment}\), \(N=0\) almost surely, so every randomized action has a distribution independent of \(\rho\).  Put \(t_-=a-br=h(r)\) and \(t_+=a+br=h(-r)\).  For any randomized endpoint action \(D\), the triangle inequality gives pointwise
\[
 |D-t_-|+|D-t_+|\geq |t_+-t_-|=2br.
\]
Taking expectations and then the larger of the two endpoint risks yields
\[
 \sup_{\rho\in[-r,r]}\mathbb E_{0,\rho}|D-h(\rho)|
 \geq \frac12\left\{\mathbb E|D-t_-|+\mathbb E|D-t_+|\right\}
 \geq br.
\]
The deterministic action \(D=a\) has loss \(b|\rho|\leq br\), with equality at \(\rho=\pm r\).  Thus \(R(0)=br\).

For a randomized closed interval \(I\subseteq\mathcal A=[t_-,t_+]\), the same absence of data makes its law independent of \(\rho\).  The elementary indicator representation of interval length and nonnegative integration give
\[
 \mathbb E\operatorname{len}(I)
 =\int_{t_-}^{t_+}\Pr\{t\in I\}\,dt.
\]
Honesty requires the integrand to be at least \(1-\alpha\) for every \(t=h(\rho)\in[t_-,t_+]\), because \(h\) maps \([-r,r]\) bijectively onto that interval.  Hence
\[
 \mathbb E\operatorname{len}(I)\geq (t_+-t_-)(1-\alpha)=2br(1-\alpha).
\]
This lower bound is attained by reporting \(\mathcal A\) with probability \(1-\alpha\) and the degenerate interval \(\{a\}\) with probability \(\alpha\), using parameter-free randomization.  Every target value other than \(a\) is then covered with probability \(1-\alpha\), while \(a\) is covered with probability one, and the expected length is \(2br(1-\alpha)\).  Therefore \(C_\alpha(0)=2br(1-\alpha)\).

Now fix any \(\lambda>0\), condition the experiment of \(\mathrm{def{:}marked\mbox{-}poisson\mbox{-}experiment}\) on exactly one mark, and denote that mark by \(S\).  (The resulting conditional experiment does not depend on \(\lambda\).)  Then
\[
 \Pr_\rho(S=s)=\frac{1+sc\rho}{2},\qquad s\in\{-1,1\}.
\]
For endpoint estimation, transform an action \(D\in[a-b,a+b]\) to \(q=(a-D)/b\in[-1,1]\).  The loss obeys
\[
 |D-h(\rho)|=b|q-\rho|.
\]
Projection of \(q\) onto \([-r,r]\) cannot increase \(|q-\rho|\) for any \(\rho\in[-r,r]\).  Next apply reflection symmetrization: mix a rule with the rule obtained by replacing \(S\) by \(-S\) and its action \(q\) by \(-q\).  At \(\rho\), the symmetrized risk is the average of the original risks at \(\rho\) and \(-\rho\), so its worst risk is no larger.  It is therefore enough for a lower bound to consider equivariant rules.  Such a rule is described by a random variable \(Q\in[-r,r]\): conditionally on \(S=1\) output \(Q\), and conditionally on \(S=-1\) output a variable distributed as \(-Q\).  Let \(m=\mathbb E Q\).  Its correlation-scale risks at \(0\) and \(r\) are
\[
 \mathcal R(0)=\mathbb E|Q|\geq m
\]
and, using \(Q\in[-r,r]\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathcal R(r)
 &=\mathbb E\left[\frac{1+cr}{2}|Q-r|+\frac{1-cr}{2}|-Q-r|\right]\\
 &=\mathbb E\left[\frac{1+cr}{2}(r-Q)+\frac{1-cr}{2}(r+Q)\right]
 =r-crm.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Set \(t=r/(1+cr)\), so that \(r-crt=t\).  If \(m\geq t\), then \(\mathcal R(0)\geq t\); if \(m<t\), then \(\mathcal R(r)=r-crm>r-crt=t\).  Thus every rule has worst correlation-scale absolute risk at least \(t\).

For attainment, use \(q=tS\).  By reflection symmetry it suffices to take \(x=|\rho|\in[0,r]\).  Direct substitution gives
\[
 \mathcal R(x)=
 \begin{cases}
 t-cx^2,&0\leq x\leq t,\\
 x(1-ct),&t\leq x\leq r.
 \end{cases}
\]
The first expression is at most \(t\).  Since \(ct<1\), the second is increasing in \(x\) and is at most
\[
 r(1-ct)=r-crt=t.
\]
Hence the one-mark minimax endpoint risk is \(bt=br/(1+cr)\).

It remains to solve the one-mark honest-interval problem.  Map every endpoint interval \(I\subseteq\mathcal A\) to
\[
 J=\{(a-y)/b:y\in I\}\subseteq[-r,r].
\]
Then \(h(\rho)\in I\) if and only if \(\rho\in J\), and \(\operatorname{len}(I)=b\operatorname{len}(J)\).  Reflection symmetrization of an arbitrary honest rule preserves honesty and replaces its expected-length function at \(\rho\) by the average of the original functions at \(\rho\) and \(-\rho\); hence it cannot increase worst expected length.  Under a symmetric rule, the conditional law of \(J\) given \(S=-1\) is the reflection of its conditional law given \(S=1\), so the two conditional expected lengths agree and the unconditional expected length is constant in \(\rho\).

Let \(J_+\) have the conditional law given \(S=1\), and for \(0<x\leq r\) define
\[
 u(x)=\Pr\{x\in J_+\},\qquad v(x)=\Pr\{-x\in J_+\}.
\]
Honesty at \(\rho=x\) is exactly
\[
 (1+cx)u(x)+(1-cx)v(x)\geq 2(1-\alpha).
\]
Assume \(cr\leq1-2\alpha\).  Then \(1-cx>0\) and \(1+cx\leq2(1-\alpha)\) for \(0<x\leq r\).  Since \(0\leq u(x)\leq1\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 2(1-\alpha)
 &\leq (1-cx)\{u(x)+v(x)\}+2cx\,u(x)\\
 &\leq (1-cx)\{u(x)+v(x)\}+2cx,
 \end{aligned}
\]
and therefore
\[
 u(x)+v(x)\geq 2-\frac{2\alpha}{1-cx}.
\]
Integrating inclusion indicators over \([-r,r]\) gives the common conditional expected length
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E\operatorname{len}(J_+)
 &=\int_0^r\{u(x)+v(x)\}\,dx\\
 &\geq\int_0^r\left(2-\frac{2\alpha}{1-cx}\right)dx
 =2r+\frac{2\alpha}{c}\log(1-cr).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Because symmetrization cannot increase the original worst expected length, this is a lower bound for every honest one-mark rule.

For attainability, the condition \(cr\leq1-2\alpha\) ensures \(2\alpha/(1-cr)\leq1\).  Define a random variable \(T\in[0,r]\) by the distribution function
\[
 \Pr(T\leq t)=\frac{2\alpha}{1-ct},\qquad 0\leq t<r,
\]
and set \(\Pr(T\leq r)=1\).  This is a valid distribution: it has mass \(2\alpha\) at zero, is increasing on \((0,r)\), and has the nonnegative remaining mass \(1-2\alpha/(1-cr)\) at \(r\).  In particular,
\[
 \Pr(T\geq x)=1-\frac{2\alpha}{1-cx},\qquad 0<x\leq r.
\]
Given \(S=1\), report \(J=[-T,r]\); given \(S=-1\), report \(J=[-r,T]\), with fresh randomization having the displayed law.  For \(0<x\leq r\), its coverage at \(\rho=x\) is
\[
 \frac{1+cx}{2}+\frac{1-cx}{2}\Pr(T\geq x)
 =\frac{1+cx}{2}+\frac{1-cx}{2}-\alpha
 =1-\alpha.
\]
Coverage at \(-x\) is the same by reflection, and coverage at zero is one because both reported intervals contain zero.  Thus the rule is uniformly honest, including at the boundary points.  Its conditional expected correlation-scale length is
\[
 r+\mathbb ET
 =r+\int_0^r\Pr(T\geq x)\,dx
 =2r+\frac{2\alpha}{c}\log(1-cr).
\]
Mapping back through \(I=a-bJ\) multiplies length by \(b\).  The lower bound and this attaining interval rule prove that the one-mark minimax expected endpoint-interval length is
\[
 b\left\{2r+\frac{2\alpha}{c}\log(1-cr)\right\}.
\]
